overview.prompt: A client newly diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis asks which tissue the disease mainly attacks. Which response is accurate?

options.text: The bone marrow of long bones
The tendons around the shoulders
The cartilage of weight-bearing joints
The synovial lining of the joints

overview.rationale: RA is a systemic autoimmune disease that primarily affects synovial joints; persistent synovitis then damages cartilage, bone, and supporting tissues. It does not mainly target weight-bearing cartilage, bone marrow, or shoulder tendons.

overview.prompt: A client asks how RA causes joint erosion. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Mechanical wear slowly thins cartilage over decades
Inflamed synovium (pannus) erodes cartilage and bone
Bacteria invade the joint space and destroy bone
Uric acid crystals deposit and wear down cartilage

overview.rationale: Thickened inflammatory synovial tissue forms pannus, and enzymes and osteoclasts erode cartilage and bone. Crystals describe gout, wear describes OA, and infection describes septic arthritis.

overview.prompt: Which extra-articular manifestations can occur in RA? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rheumatoid skin nodules
Tophi on the ear helix
Scleritis of the eye
Pericarditis of the heart
Interstitial lung disease

overview.rationale: RA can affect lungs, heart, eyes (scleritis), vessels, and skin (nodules). Tophi are deposits seen in gout.

manifestations.prompt: Which morning-stiffness history most suggests inflammatory arthritis such as RA?

options.text: Stiffness that lasts a long time after waking
Stiffness that occurs in the evening hours
Stiffness that appears mainly after exercise
Stiffness that eases within a few minutes

manifestations.rationale: Prolonged stiffness after rest (often more than an hour in the morning) suggests inflammatory joint disease. Brief stiffness that eases quickly is more typical of OA, and stiffness tied to exercise or evenings is not the inflammatory pattern described.

manifestations.prompt: When examining a client with typical RA, which joints does the nurse expect to be spared?

options.text: The radiocarpal (wrist) joints
Proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints
Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints
Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints

manifestations.rationale: DIP joints are usually spared in typical RA. MCPs, PIPs, and wrists (plus MTPs) are common sites, so they are expected to be involved.

manifestations.prompt: A client with long-standing RA has fingers with the PIP joint hyperextended and the DIP joint flexed. How is this documented?

options.text: Ulnar drift deformity
Boutonnière deformity
Swan-neck deformity
Mallet finger deformity

manifestations.rationale: Swan-neck deformity is PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion; boutonnière is the reverse. Ulnar drift is deviation toward the little finger, and a mallet finger is DIP droop without PIP hyperextension.

manifestations.prompt: A client with established RA reports neck pain and new tingling and weakness in both arms. What is the nurse’s best action?

options.text: Teach neck range-of-motion exercises at home
Arrange urgent evaluation of the cervical spine
Treat it as a routine flare with an NSAID dose
Apply moist heat and reassess at the next visit

manifestations.rationale: Cervical-spine disease can cause instability/myelopathy in established RA, so new neurological symptoms need prompt evaluation. Treating it as a routine flare or exercising the neck is unsafe.

risk.prompt: A client with anti-CCP-positive RA asks what they can change to improve outcomes. Which risk factor is most important to address?

options.text: Daily caffeine intake
Cigarette smoking
Cold weather exposure
A high-protein diet

risk.rationale: Smoking is an important modifiable risk, particularly for antibody-positive disease. The other factors are not listed RA risks.

risk.prompt: A client has had persistent swollen finger joints for several weeks. When should a DMARD ideally be started if RA is confirmed?

options.text: Promptly, early in the course of the disease
After a long trial of NSAID therapy fails
After joint erosions appear on an X-ray
After a period of watchful observation

risk.rationale: Start a DMARD promptly once indicated, ideally early (within 3 months of persistent symptom onset). Waiting for erosions, failed NSAIDs, or a period of observation loses the window to prevent damage.

risk.prompt: A client has persistent swelling of several small hand joints, but RF and anti-CCP are negative. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Repeat antibody tests in a year
Reassurance that RA is excluded
Prompt rheumatology referral
Referral once the ESR rises

risk.rationale: Persistent small-joint synovitis needs prompt rheumatology referral even with normal ESR/CRP or negative RF/anti-CCP. Seronegative RA exists, so reassurance, delayed retesting, or waiting for ESR to rise would delay treatment.

diagnostics.prompt: Which laboratory result is relatively specific for RA and may indicate higher erosive risk?

options.text: Antinuclear antibody (ANA)
Rheumatoid factor (RF)
Anti-CCP antibody (ACPA)
Sedimentation rate (ESR)

diagnostics.rationale: Anti-CCP is relatively specific for RA and, at higher titers, can indicate greater erosive risk. RF is less specific, ANA is not RA-specific, and ESR is a general inflammation marker.

diagnostics.prompt: A client with classic RA findings has negative RF and anti-CCP. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Negative results can rule out RA
Positive ANA is needed to confirm RA
The tests should be repeated weekly
Both can be negative in genuine RA

diagnostics.rationale: Both RF and ACPA can be negative in genuine RA, so negative serology does not exclude it. ANA is not RA-specific, and weekly repeat testing is not indicated.

diagnostics.prompt: A client with RA has a hot, swollen knee, and synovial fluid shows an inflammatory WBC count. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Infection is excluded by an inflammatory range
Crystals are unlikely with active RA
Septic arthritis and gout are not ruled out
The result confirms a routine RA flare

diagnostics.rationale: An inflammatory WBC range does not rule out septic arthritis or gout; Gram stain/culture and crystal analysis are needed, and they can coexist.

diagnostics.prompt: Before a client starts a TNF inhibitor for RA, which screening specifically addresses the risk of reactivating latent infection?

options.text: Thyroid function panel
TB and hepatitis B screening
Uric acid and kidney panel
Bone density (DEXA) scan

diagnostics.rationale: Screen for TB and hepatitis B because TNF-inhibitor therapy can reactivate infection. Renal and other drug-specific safety tests may also be needed, but they do not substitute for this infectious-disease screening.

medical.prompt: A client with newly diagnosed active RA asks which medicine is usually started first to control the disease. Which is the common initial anchor DMARD?

options.text: Tofacitinib
Methotrexate
Prednisone
Ibuprofen

medical.rationale: Methotrexate is commonly the initial anchor DMARD for active RA. NSAIDs and steroids relieve symptoms, and JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib are used after an inadequate response.

medical.prompt: A client has taken methotrexate for several months with little improvement. Per current EULAR guidance, what should happen?

options.text: Continue it unchanged for a full year
Stop DMARDs and switch to NSAIDs
The treatment should be adjusted
Wait until erosions are visible

medical.rationale: EULAR calls for adjusting treatment when improvement is insufficient early (by about 3 months) or the target is not reached (by 6 months). Waiting longer, relying on NSAIDs, or waiting for erosions allows damage.

medical.prompt: A client with RA says, “Ibuprofen controls my pain, so I don’t need methotrexate.” What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “NSAIDs ease pain but don’t prevent joint damage.”
“That’s right; NSAIDs stop the disease process.”
“NSAIDs work as well as methotrexate long term.”
“You can switch to NSAIDs once pain is gone.”

medical.rationale: NSAIDs relieve pain/inflammation but do not replace DMARD protection against damage. The other responses wrongly suggest NSAIDs modify the disease.

medications.prompt: A client is starting methotrexate for RA. How should the nurse teach the dosing schedule?

options.text: Once weekly on the same day
On days with joint pain
Once daily with breakfast
Twice a day with meals

medications.rationale: Methotrexate for RA is taken once weekly; accidental daily dosing can be fatal. Daily or as-needed dosing is unsafe.

medications.prompt: A client says they have been taking methotrexate every day this week. What is the nurse’s priority action?

options.text: Arrange urgent medical or poison-service review
Tell the client to skip next week’s dose instead
Advise extra folic acid and fluids at home
Recheck labs at the next routine clinic visit

medications.rationale: If daily dosing is suspected, seek urgent medical/poison-service assessment rather than waiting; daily dosing can be fatal.

medications.prompt: A client has started hydroxychloroquine. Which monitoring should the nurse make sure is arranged?

options.text: Baseline and ongoing bone marrow review
Baseline and ongoing hearing tests
Baseline and ongoing uric acid levels
Baseline and ongoing retinal screening

medications.rationale: Retinal toxicity can be irreversible, so baseline and ongoing retinal screening is needed. The other tests are not HCQ monitoring.

medications.prompt: A client who took leflunomide now plans pregnancy. What may be required?

options.text: Doubling the folic acid dose for a week
No action, because it clears within days
Simply stopping the tablets the day before
A supervised drug-elimination procedure

medications.rationale: The active metabolite persists a long time; pregnancy planning may require supervised elimination, commonly with cholestyramine (or activated charcoal). Stopping tablets does not immediately eliminate exposure.

medications.prompt: A client is prescribed tofacitinib and asks if it is a biologic injection. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “It is an oral targeted synthetic DMARD.”
“It is an NSAID that relieves joint pain.”
“It is a biologic given as an IV infusion.”
“It is a TNF inhibitor given by injection.”

medications.rationale: Tofacitinib is an oral targeted synthetic (JAK) medicine, not a biologic or TNF blocker. It is not injected or infused, and it is a DMARD rather than an NSAID.

nonpharmacological.prompt: A client with RA has stiff hands every morning. Which comfort measure should the nurse suggest?

options.text: Forceful stretching of stiff joints
Moist warmth for morning stiffness
Complete rest until stiffness resolves
Ice packs on the hands each morning

nonpharmacological.rationale: Moist warmth can help morning stiffness; wrapped cold is for a hot, swollen joint. Forcing painful joints or prolonged rest is avoided.

nonpharmacological.prompt: A client with RA is having a flare. Which activity advice is best?

options.text: Splint the joints continuously until it settles
Stay in bed until the flare has fully settled
Keep the usual exercise intensity to build strength
Modify loading and rest more, but avoid immobility

nonpharmacological.rationale: During a flare, modify loading and allow more rest without prolonged complete immobilization. Bed rest or continuous splinting worsens stiffness and deconditioning, and unchanged intensity overloads inflamed joints.

adverse-effects.prompt: A client on methotrexate develops a new dry cough and shortness of breath. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Advise cough syrup and recheck in a month
Reassure that this is expected and harmless
Report promptly for possible pneumonitis or infection
Increase the methotrexate to control RA lung disease

adverse-effects.rationale: Methotrexate can cause pneumonitis or other lung toxicity, and new cough/dyspnea also raises infection or RA lung concerns. Reassurance, a higher dose, or waiting a month would delay evaluation.

adverse-effects.prompt: A client taking adalimumab feels very unwell with chills but has a temperature of 37.2°C (99°F). How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Infection is ruled out by the temperature
The biologic should be doubled
Serious infection is still possible
This is an expected injection reaction

adverse-effects.rationale: Fever may be blunted on biologics, so an afebrile patient is not automatically infection-free. This is not an injection-site reaction, and the dose should never be increased by the nurse.

adverse-effects.prompt: A client says, “I take my naproxen with milk, so I can’t get an ulcer.” What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “That’s right; milk can fully protect the stomach.”
“Ulcers mainly occur with COX-2 inhibitors.”
“Milk can ease upset but doesn’t prevent ulcers.”
“Taking it at bedtime would also prevent ulcers.”

adverse-effects.rationale: Food or milk may reduce stomach upset but does not prevent ulcers or bleeding. COX-2 agents reduce but do not eliminate GI risk, and dose timing does not prevent ulcers.

nutrition.prompt: A client with RA asks about diet. Which eating approach may support symptoms and heart health?

options.text: A diet used in place of DMARDs
A very low-fat, low-protein diet
A Mediterranean-style pattern
A strict grain-free elimination diet

nutrition.rationale: A Mediterranean-style pattern may support symptoms and cardiometabolic health but does not replace DMARDs. Restrictive diets can compromise nutrition.

nutrition.prompt: A client asks why folic acid is prescribed with methotrexate. What is the best explanation?

options.text: To make daily methotrexate safe
To reduce methotrexate adverse effects
To strengthen methotrexate’s effect
To replace liver test monitoring

nutrition.rationale: Folic acid on the prescribed schedule reduces adverse effects; it does not eliminate marrow/liver risks or make daily methotrexate safe.

nutrition.prompt: A client with RA has a low hemoglobin. Which approach should the nurse take?

options.text: Start iron supplements right away
Increase red meat intake to correct it
Ignore it as an expected part of RA
Investigate the cause before treating

nutrition.rationale: Investigate anemia rather than giving iron for all RA-related anemia, because inflammation and iron deficiency are different problems. Starting iron or diet changes without a cause, or ignoring it, is not appropriate.

assessment.prompt: When reviewing methotrexate safety with a client, which detail is most important to confirm?

options.text: The weekly dose day and the folate schedule
Which OTC vitamins the client has stopped
The time of day the client usually eats lunch
Whether it is taken with water or juice

assessment.rationale: Confirm the once-weekly methotrexate day, actual dose, folate schedule, and missed or extra doses because accidental daily dosing can be fatal. Also reconcile OTC vitamins and supplements for potential interactions; the weekly dosing and folate plan remain the central safety detail in this question.

assessment.prompt: A client with RA and known cervical-spine instability is scheduled for surgery under general anesthesia. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document it in the nursing notes alone
Teach neck-strengthening exercises first
Alert the procedural team before the case
Hold the RA medicines without an order

assessment.rationale: Alert the procedural and anesthesia teams to known instability because airway manipulation can be dangerous. Stopping medicines independently, teaching exercises, or documenting without telling the team does not protect the client.

diagnoses.prompt: A client with RA is taking methotrexate and a TNF inhibitor. Which nursing diagnosis is most directly supported by the medicines?

options.text: Risk for bleeding
Impaired swallowing
Risk for aspiration
Risk for infection

diagnoses.rationale: Risk for infection relates to selected immunosuppressive therapy and individual risk factors. The other diagnoses are not supported by these medicines.

diagnoses.prompt: A client with RA misses lab appointments. The nurse learns the client cannot afford transport. Which approach to the learning-needs diagnosis is correct?

options.text: Address cost and access barriers
Document it as nonadherence
Repeat the same teaching session
Label it as lack of knowledge

diagnoses.rationale: Avoid assuming lack of knowledge when the real barrier is cost or disability; address practical barriers instead.

priorities.prompt: A client with RA presents with one very hot, swollen knee and a temperature of 38.6°C (101.5°F). What is the nurse’s first priority?

options.text: Give the next scheduled methotrexate dose
Treat it as a routine RA flare at home
Assess for a septic joint and escalate
Apply moist heat to the swollen knee

priorities.rationale: A very hot, swollen joint with fever in a client with RA needs urgent assessment for septic arthritis rather than an assumption of a routine flare. Check clinical stability and escalate for appropriate joint-fluid and infection evaluation. Routine comfort measures or administering the next immunosuppressant dose must not delay that assessment.

priorities.prompt: A client with early synovitis has negative antibodies and a normal hand X-ray. What should the nurse advocate for?

options.text: NSAIDs alone and no referral
Repeat X-ray in one year
Waiting for erosions to appear
Prompt rheumatology referral

priorities.rationale: To protect against irreversible damage, do not delay referral for negative antibodies or a normal X-ray, since early films may be normal. Waiting for erosions or relying on NSAIDs alone allows damage to progress.

plan.prompt: Which overall aim best fits an RA plan of care?

options.text: A normal ESR as the main treatment target
Avoiding DMARDs to keep side effects to a minimum
Remission or low disease activity with function
Brief morning stiffness as the single goal

plan.rationale: Aim for sustained remission/low activity and meaningful function rather than a single laboratory or stiffness cutoff. Avoiding DMARDs would allow joint damage.

plan.prompt: Which outcome best shows the medication-safety goal is met for a client on methotrexate?

options.text: Stops folate once mouth ulcers heal
Takes methotrexate daily for better control
States the weekly methotrexate and folate plan
Skips lab tests whenever feeling well

plan.rationale: The goal includes demonstrating the weekly methotrexate/folate distinction and completing monitoring. Daily dosing and skipped labs are unsafe.

interventions.prompt: A client with RA has an acutely inflamed wrist. Which joint-care approach is best?

options.text: Lift weights to build up wrist strength
Keep the wrist immobilized for several weeks
Push through full range despite severe pain
Avoid heavy loading but keep gentle movement

interventions.rationale: Avoid excessive loading of acutely inflamed joints and also prolonged inactivity that worsens stiffness/deconditioning. Forcing range through severe pain risks injury.

interventions.prompt: Before discharge, a client with RA has hand deformities and fatigue. Which intervention best supports continuity of care?

options.text: Link to the treating team and community resources
Leave follow-up arrangements up to the client
Provide the standard small-print instructions
Give a long verbal briefing with no written plan

interventions.rationale: Link the client with the interdisciplinary team and resources such as the Arthritis Foundation, and use accessible written instructions for hand, vision, and fatigue needs. Leaving follow-up to the client or using inaccessible materials undermines continuity.

education.prompt: Which statement by a client taking methotrexate shows correct understanding?

options.text: “I take it once a week, with folate as prescribed.”
“I can double my methotrexate dose on bad days.”
“I take methotrexate each morning with breakfast.”
“Folic acid can be used in place of methotrexate.”

education.rationale: Methotrexate for RA is once weekly, with folate taken as separately prescribed. Daily or doubled dosing is dangerous.

education.prompt: A client taking methotrexate discovers she is pregnant. What should she be taught to do?

options.text: Contact the team promptly
Wait until the next routine visit
Stop folic acid immediately
Double the methotrexate dose

education.rationale: Contact the team promptly for pregnancy exposure to methotrexate or leflunomide; methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy.

evaluation.prompt: A client’s CRP is normal, but several joints remain swollen. How should the nurse evaluate disease control?

options.text: The normal CRP proves remission
Swelling matters less once CRP is normal
Morning stiffness alone shows success
No single marker proves remission

evaluation.rationale: No single marker or stiffness duration proves success; joint examination and activity measures are reviewed with ESR/CRP.

evaluation.prompt: A client with long-standing ulnar drift asks if treatment will straighten the fingers. How should the nurse frame evaluation?

options.text: Judge success solely by deformity change
Promise the deformities will fully reverse
Track progression without promising reversal
Stop evaluating since damage already exists

evaluation.rationale: Assess progression over time rather than promising every existing deformity will reverse; function and ADLs are tracked.
